title: Minecraft's real random numbers
plain: Minecraft Java builds its world from a simple 48-bit counter that spits out numbers from a seed. Copying that recipe takes about 15 lines of Rust and needs no libraries, so a real Java seed gives the real game's numbers.
why: Starting from the true generator means the route we plan is for the real world, not a toy one.
done_when: The counter, started from known seeds, prints exactly the numbers Java prints.

title: Mining fixes the count locally
plain: When one block is mined, only the four tiny 2-by-2 windows around it can change the Euler score. Checking those four spots replaces re-counting the whole map.
why: The planner can try thousands of dig-here ideas per second because each costs four checks.
done_when: After mining or placing a block, the quick update equals a full recount.

title: Exact planning with A*
plain: A* is a search that skips any route it can prove is slower, guided by the tech tree (what you must craft before what). It always returns the fastest plan, instead of guessing with random rollouts.
why: An exact planner cannot lose to a random baseline, which is the claim the speedrun has to win.
done_when: A* route cost equals the slow ground-truth shortest-path cost on every fixed seed.

title: Website with no framework
plain: The Rust standard library can already listen for web requests, so the site needs about 30 lines instead of a web framework with around 100 extra libraries.
why: Fewer libraries means faster builds and less memory on a machine with 3.3 GB free.
done_when: Asking the local server on port 7740 for the charts file returns the chart data.
